Estonia to close Russian border crossings after attempted arson attack

Nov 15 (Reuters) – Estonia will close all its border crossing points with Russia from December 1, its foreign minister said on Sunday, following a suspected sabotage attack on an Estonian defence company that Tallinn blamed on Moscow.

Estonian authorities detained eight people overnight on suspicion of an attempted arson attack on drone maker Threod Systems that they said had been ordered by Russia’s GRU military intelligence service.

There was no immediate comment from Moscow on Estonia’s accusations or its decision to shut the border crossings. Moscow has regularly denied accusations by European authorities of involvement in sabotage operations.

Show Full Article

“Russia must understand that hostile actions against Estonia come with consequences,” Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said in a post on X.

He did not specify how long the border closure would last or if an end date had been set.

Estonia, a NATO and European Union member state and a strong supporter of Ukraine, currently has three open border crossings with Russia at Narva, Luhamaa and Koidula, which admit pedestrians and freight, according to Estonian public broadcaster ERR.

(Reporting by Andrius Sytas in Vilnius, Writing by Terje Solsvik, Editing by Louise Heavens and Gareth Jones)

ASEAN, China fail to conclude South China Sea code of conduct

Reuters

By Mikhail Flores and Nestor Corrales MANILA, Nov 15 (Reuters) – ASEAN and China were unable to conclude negotiations on a long-delayed South China Sea code of conduct under the Philippines’ chairmanship, despite reaching provisional agreement on about 80% of the draft, Manila’s foreign minister said on Sunday.

Negotiations on an ASEAN-China Code of Conduct in the South China Sea have dragged on for over two decades, but the Philippines, as current chair, had committed to speed up those talks and conclude the code this year.

“There is no conclusion yet,” Philippine foreign minister Ma. Theresa Lazaro told a press conference at a summit of the 11-member Association of Southeast Asian Nations in Manila, adding that several key issues remain unresolved, including questions over whether the code would be legally binding.

Show Full Article

“The ASEAN countries plus China have also different views on how things are,” she added.

China’s Southeast Asian neighbours want the code to be grounded in international law, which they have repeatedly accused Beijing of disregarding as it asserts its sovereignty over nearly all of the South China Sea.

Beijing maintains that its actions in the South China Sea have been lawful and professional.

OVERLAPPING MARITIME CLAIMS

China’s extensive maritime claims overlap with the exclusive economic zones of Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines and Vietnam, making a functional code essential to preventing any escalation of tensions and managing incidents at sea.

An international arbitration tribunal ruled in 2016 that China’s sweeping claims have no basis under international law, a decision that Beijing rejects.

Manila and Beijing have been locked in a series of maritime confrontations in recent years, with the Philippines accusing China of repeated aggressive actions inside its exclusive economic zone, including dangerous manoeuvres, water‑cannoning and disrupting resupply missions.

China, for its part, has accused the Philippines of intruding into what it claims as its territory.

Analysts say the disagreements are not only between ASEAN and China.

Collin Koh, a senior fellow at Singapore’s S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies, said divisions among ASEAN members, including over the geographical scope of the code, had also slowed negotiations.

“Other than Beijing, intramural divergences within ASEAN also play a significant role,” he said.

Koh said the remaining differences would be difficult to resolve and would require “major concessions” from the various parties.

Singapore will inherit the task of trying to secure agreement on the code of conduct when it assumes the ASEAN chairmanship next year.

(Writing by Karen Lema, editing by Gareth Jones)

By Michael Kahn PRAGUE, Nov 15 (Reuters) – Tens of thousands of Czechs protested in Prague on Sunday against a government plan to cut a public media fee and move funding to the state budget – a policy critics say would dent the broadcasters’ independence and viability.

Opposition parties compared the proposals in an October bill to changes in Hungary under former Prime Minister Viktor Orban, who built an array of pro-government media.

Local authorities had estimated hundreds of thousands would attend the rally days before the November 17 holiday commemorating the 1989 Velvet Revolution that swept away Communist rule and propelled dissident playwright Vaclav Havel to power.

Show Full Article

The front section near the stage in Letna park overlooking the Czech capital filled quickly as protesters clogged nearby metro stations. Many wore pointed hats folded out of newspapers as tribute to an animated character who has introduced Czech Television’s nightly children’s bedtime stories for decades.

The populist government of billionaire Prime Minister Andrej Babis, backed by the far-right SPD and eurosceptic Motorists parties, accuses private and public media of bias.

The coalition backs a bill that would cancel a 205-crown ($9.26) monthly household broadcasting fee currently used for funding. The bill has passed a preliminary vote and awaits further debate.

Czech public television and radio workers escalated the fight with a one-day strike earlier in November that led to broadcast curbs and protests backed by artists and students.

Critics say the funding shift to the budget would undercut the media’s relationship with paying viewers and make the sector susceptible to political pressure.

A 15% financing cut proposed as part of the change would bring television’s nominal budget to the level of 2008 and radio’s to 2005. Media say that is unworkable.

Babis says the government is merely meeting a promise to lighten the financial burden on people.

($1 = 22.1280 Czech crowns)

(Reporting by Michael Kahn, Editing by Andrew Cawthorne)

Yemeni government force retreats from strait in major setback in war against Houthis

Reuters

By Mohammed Ghobari Nov 15 (Reuters) – Yemeni government forces announced on Sunday they were withdrawing from the area near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait to focus on a defence of their main base in Aden, in a major setback for the Saudi-backed campaign against the Iran-aligned Houthis.

The announcement signalled the apparent end of a six-week government counteroffensive to reclaim the coast near the mouth of the Red Sea, seized by the Houthis in September in a lightning advance that squeezed oil exports.

Sunday’s announcement of a government retreat raises the prospect of new Houthi advances towards Aden, and underscores the predicament faced by Saudi Arabia in trying to stop the Houthis’ drone and missile attacks on the kingdom. The government forces have been based in Aden on the southern coast since 2015 after the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa.

Show Full Article

Houthi gains in Yemen and attacks on Saudi Arabia and Red Sea shipping in recent months have strengthened the position of Iran in the wider Middle East conflict launched by the United States and Israel in February.

“The Southern Armed Forces announce the implementation of a redeployment operation for its forces from Dhubab Airport and the Bab el-Mandeb area, west of Taiz Governorate,” the main military force fighting for Yemen’s government in the south of the country said in a statement.

“This step is taken based on the priority of securing the capital, Aden, and the neighbouring governorates, as well as strengthening the front lines and addressing existing threats.”

There was no immediate response from the Houthis, or from Saudi Arabia, the Yemeni government’s main international ally.

HOUTHI GAINS

Yemen’s decade-long civil war, which had been dormant since 2022, abruptly reignited this summer as a spillover from the Iran conflict. The Houthis made rapid gains to capture the coast along the Red Sea and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait that controls access to it, while besieging government forces in Taiz, the country’s third-biggest city, in mountains above the approach to Aden.

A Saudi-backed government offensive last month rapidly retook key positions around the strait, notably Dhubab, but failed to drive the Houthis entirely away from the area or to retake the city of al-Mocha further up the coast.

The Houthis have responded by intensifying drone and missile attacks on Saudi Arabia, grounding flights with strikes on its main airports as well as setting global energy markets on edge by targeting energy facilities.

They also made significant advances in the highland areas north of Aden, cutting off Taiz in early October and putting increased pressure on the disparate coalition of forces fighting for the internationally recognised government.

GOVERNMENT FORCES STILL TRYING TO PUSH HOUTHIS FROM COAST

Around Bab el-Mandeb the government forces have redeployed to al-Suqyah, just south of Dhubab and 150 km (95 miles) west of Aden, but are still trying to push the Houthis from coastal areas nearby, Yemeni military sources said.

In the highlands south of Taiz, the Houthis are positioned just outside the district of Tur al-Bahah in Lahj governorate, about 80 km (50 miles) from Aden.

The Houthi gains around Taiz, which has become the fiercest front of the civil war, undermined the government campaign around Bab el-Mandeb, the military sources said.

Fighting is still intensifying around the western region of Taiz, with humanitarian conditions worsening. The city, which hosts about half of the 300,000 people displaced across Yemen by the latest fighting, remains besieged. Aid supplies are unable to enter, and civilians are unable to leave.

The Houthis have meanwhile released 600 prisoners, the International Committee of the Red Cross said on Sunday.

(Reporting by Mohammed Ghobari; Additional reporting by Reyam Mukhashaf in Aden; Writing by Nayera Abdallah and Angus McDowall; Editing by William Mallard and Peter Graff)
